title: The Golden Age of Athens
tagline: A statesman, a philosopher, and a king debate the soul of democracy.

scenes.text: Athens, 450 BCE. The city shimmers at the height of its glory. The Parthenon rises on the Acropolis. Sophocles writes his tragedies. Democracy shapes every argument in the agora. And the man steering this golden age has at his side the most remarkable woman in Greece.

scenes.speaker: Pericles
scenes.text: Our constitution is called democracy because power is in the hands of the many, not the few. We do not imitate our neighbours — we are a pattern to others. Athens is the school of all Greece.

scenes.speaker: Aspasia
scenes.text: And yet, Pericles, women may not vote, may not speak in the Assembly, may not be citizens. How free is a democracy that silences half its people? Tell me — does truth only count when a man speaks it?

scenes.speaker: Pericles
scenes.text: You argue like a philosopher and counsel like a strategos. It is why I love you — and why Athens both admires and despises us for it.

challenge.instruction: Not every Athenian wants the allies' tribute spent on temples. Thucydides son of Melesias is stirring up the countryside — tour the demes of Attica and win them for Pericles' building programme.
challenge.fact: The quarrel over the building programme was settled by ostracism around 443 BCE: Thucydides son of Melesias was sent into exile for ten years, and Pericles was elected general year after year until his death.

scenes.text: Aspasia of Miletus ran a salon in Athens where the greatest minds of the age gathered. Socrates came. Alcibiades came. She discussed rhetoric, politics, and philosophy with them as an equal. Her foreign birth placed her outside Athenian law — and ironically, gave her freedoms Athenian women did not have.

scenes.speaker: Aspasia
scenes.text: A city that silences half its people silences half its wisdom. Tell me, Socrates — is it Athens that is great, or the minds Athens has not yet learned to silence?

scenes.speaker: Pericles
scenes.text: They say I speak well. They are wrong. I speak what she has taught me. Aspasia sees through to the heart of every argument. My Funeral Oration — the words that will outlast stone — I did not write alone.

params.title: The Owls of Athens
params.intro: Strike Laurion silver from tiny obols up to the four-drachma owl — and on to the talents of the treasury.
params.fact: Athens struck its silver tetradrachms, stamped with Athena and her owl, from the mines of Laurion. In 454 BCE the treasury of the Delian League was moved from Delos to Athens, and Pericles spent its tribute on the Acropolis.
params.twistText: Laurion silver: a raw lump of silver merges with any coin and lifts it one tier — but two lumps will not merge. Save them for the coin that needs them.

challenge.instruction: Aspasia's salon talks philosophy, but the city outside runs on silver. Strike Laurion silver up to the owl that carries Athens' name across the Aegean.
challenge.fact: Athenian owls were trusted so widely that they were imitated from Egypt to Arabia. 'Owls to Athens' was a Greek saying for something pointless — Aristophanes uses it in The Birds.

scenes.text: Across the Aegean, Sparta watches Athens grow with suspicion and dread. Pleistoanax, king of Sparta, warns his council of what Athens' power will mean for Greece.

scenes.speaker: Pleistoanax
scenes.text: Athens calls her empire an alliance. She takes tribute from her allies and spends it on her own temples. If we do not act, all of Greece will be Athenian before we draw breath to protest.

challenge.instruction: Pleistoanax's warning becomes an army: in 446 BCE the Peloponnesians march into Attica. Post the Athenian archers along the road from Eleusis so the invaders cannot reach the city.
challenge.fact: Pericles dominated Athenian politics for three decades through strategic alliances and oratorical power — power that his enemies claimed was shaped by Aspasia.

challenge.instruction: Pericles must win a majority in the Athenian Assembly to fund the Parthenon from Delian League tribute. Lobby the tribes before Thucydides son of Melesias turns them.
challenge.fact: The Parthenon (447–432 BCE) was built under Pericles' direction. It took fifteen years, 20,000 workers and 13,400 blocks of Pentelic marble cut to tolerances of 0.2 mm.

scenes.text: Aspasia's enemies, unable to attack Pericles directly, dragged her before the courts on charges of impiety. It was an assault on him through her. She faced Athenian justice as a foreigner, a woman, and a partner of the most powerful man in the city.

scenes.speaker: Aspasia
scenes.text: They cannot touch Pericles directly — so they strike at me. I will not dignify their cowardice with silence. Let them carve their accusations in stone. Every word only proves they listened.

challenge.instruction: Aspasia is on trial in Athens. Defend her reputation with the right arguments before the jury.
challenge.fact: Pericles wept openly before the jury defending Aspasia — an extraordinary breach of Athenian decorum. She was acquitted. His tears won more votes than the logic.

challenge.instruction: While Aspasia's enemies attack in court, the work on the Acropolis goes on. Every column rises from numbered marble drums: push each drum onto its own base.
challenge.fact: Each Doric column of the Parthenon was built up from about ten to twelve drums of Pentelic marble, quarried on Mount Pentelikon some 16 km from the Acropolis and fluted only after the column stood. Pheidias oversaw the works for Pericles.

scenes.text: The Peloponnesian War lasted 27 years and ended in Athens' defeat. But the ideas born in this golden age — democracy, philosophy, tragedy — outlasted every army and empire that followed. And later writers credited Aspasia with some of Pericles' most famous words.

challenge.instruction: War comes at last. Pericles brings the people of Attica inside the Long Walls and lets the Spartans burn the fields — place walls and towers so no raiding party reaches the city.
challenge.fact: In the winter of 431 BCE Pericles gave the Funeral Oration for the war's first dead, as Thucydides records it: 'the whole earth is the tomb of famous men.' In Plato's Menexenus, Socrates teases that Aspasia composed it.

challenge.instruction: What outlasted the war was what Athens built and sang. Raise the Odeon of Pericles course by course, its peaked roof last.
challenge.fact: The Parthenon (447–432 BCE) was built with astonishing precision: its columns taper, its platform curves, and its lines are never quite straight — all deliberate optical corrections to make the building appear perfect to the human eye. Greek architecture and geometry were inseparable.

scenes.speaker: Pericles
scenes.text: Cicero and Chanakya hold Carthage together, and a follower stands with them. One card alone will not move them. Bring Aspasia with me, add both followers, and strike twice.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 2 · Strength in Numbers. Over two turns stack Pericles, Aspasia and both followers at Carthage, then win two attacks against the rival side.
challenge.fact: An attack compares whole sides at a location, not single cards. Two Great People and two followers in the same stat outweigh a rival who arrived first, and each win sends one rival card back to its owner's hand.
